source_text:
Ac iam, ut fecundius nequiora proueniunt, serpentibus in dies perditis moribus per uniuersum orbem sacraria ista taeterrima impiae coitionis adolescunt. eruenda prorsus haec et execranda consensio.
occultis se notis et insignibus noscunt et amant mutuo paene antequam nouerint: passim etiam inter eos uelut quaedam libidinum religio miscetur, ac se promisce appellant fratres et sorores, ut etiam non insolens stuprum intercessione sacri nominis fiat incestum. ita eorum uana et demens superstitio sceleribus gloriatur.
nec de ipsis, nisi subsisteret ueritas, maxime nefaria et honore praefanda sagax fama loqueretur. audio eos turpissimae pecudis caput [asini] consecratum inepta nescio qua persuasione uenerari: digna et nata religio talibus moribus!
alii eos ferunt ipsius antistitis ac sacerdotis colere genitalia et quasi parentis sui adorare naturam: nescio an falsa, certe occultis ac nocturnis sacris adposita suspicio! et qui hominem summo supplicio pro facinore punitum et crucis ligna feralia eorum caerimonias fabulatur, congruentia perditis sceleratisque tribuit altaria, ut id colant quod merentur.
iam de initiandis tirunculis fabula tam detestanda quam nota est. infans farre contectus, ut decipiat incautos, adponitur ei qui sacris inbuatur. is infans a tirunculo fanis superficie quasi ad innoxios ictus prouocato caecis occultisque uulneribus occiditur. huius, pro nefas! sitienter sanguinem lambunt, huius certatim membra dispertiunt, hac foederantur hostia, hac conscientia sceleris ad silentium mutuum pignerantur. haec sacra sacrilegiis omnibus taetriora.
et de conuiuio notum est; passim omnes locuntur, id etiam Cirtensis nostri testatur oratio. ad epulas sollemni die coeunt cum omnibus liberis, sororibus, matribus, sexus omnis homines et omnis aetatis. illic post multas epulas, ubi conuiuium caluit et incestae libidinis ebriatis feruor exarsit, canis, qui candelabro nexus est, iactu offulae ultra spatium lineae, qua uinctus est, ad impetum et saltum prouocatur.
sic euerso et extincto conscio lumine mpudentibus tenebris nexus infandae cupiditatis inuoluunt per incertum sortis, etsi non omnes opera, conscientia tamen pariter incesti, quoniam uoto uniuersorum adpetitur quicquid accidere potest in actu singulorum.
thought_title: The secret crimes of the Christians
orientation: Caecilius is attacking Christianity, describing its spread as a depraved secret society and detailing the alleged crimes of its initiation and feasts.
pass_a_gloss: And now, as worse things spring up more fruitfully, with morals being lost day by day, those foulest shrines of an impious union are growing throughout the whole world. This conspiracy must be utterly rooted out and cursed. They recognize each other by secret marks and signs and love each other mutually almost before they know each other: also a kind of religion of lust is mixed among them everywhere, and they call each other brothers and sisters indiscriminately, so that even not unusual debauchery becomes incest through the intercession of the sacred name. Thus their empty and mad superstition boasts of crimes. Nor would a shrewd rumor speak of them, unless the truth stood firm, as most wicked and things to be cursed before honor. I hear that they venerate the head of a most foul beast, an ass, consecrated by some foolish persuasion: a religion worthy and born for such morals! Others report that they worship the genitals of their own high priest and priest and adore the nature of their parent as it were: I do not know whether it is false, certainly a suspicion attached to hidden and nocturnal rites! And he who tells of a man punished with the highest penalty for a crime and the funereal wood of the cross as their ceremonies, assigns fitting altars to the lost and wicked, so that they worship what they deserve. Now about the initiation of novices the story is as detestable as it is well known. An infant covered with grain, to deceive the unwary, is placed before the one who is to be initiated into the rites. This infant is killed by the novice with blind and hidden wounds, after the surface of the grain has been provoked as if to harmless blows. Of this one, O wickedness! they greedily lick the blood, of this one they eagerly divide the limbs, by this victim they are bound together, by this consciousness of crime they are pledged to mutual silence. These rites are more foul than all sacrileges. And about the banquet it is well known; everyone speaks of it everywhere, the speech of our fellow citizen of Cirta also testifies to it. They come together for a feast on a solemn day with all their children, sisters, mothers, people of every sex and every age. There after much feasting, when the banquet has grown hot and the heat of incestuous lust has blazed up in the drunken ones, a dog, which is tied to a lampstand, is provoked to attack and leap by the throwing of a morsel beyond the length of the line by which it is bound. Thus when the conscious light has been overturned and extinguished, they wrap themselves in shameless darkness in the bonds of unspeakable desire by the uncertainty of lot, and even if not all in deed, nevertheless equally in consciousness of incest, since whatever can happen in the act of individuals is sought by the wish of all.

choices.english: those foulest shrines of an impious union
choices.why: Keeps the sarcastic force of sacraria (shrines) applied to Christian meeting places and the contempt of taeterrima.
rejected: those most foul sanctuaries of an impious assembly
those foulest temples of a wicked gathering

choices.english: a kind of religion of lust
choices.why: Preserves the oxymoron religio + libidinum and the hedging uelut quaedam.
rejected: a sort of worship of lusts

choices.english: through the intercession of the sacred name
choices.why: Keeps the legal-sounding intercessione and the sarcasm of sacri nominis.
rejected: by the intervention of the holy name
through the mediation of the sacred title

choices.term: digna et nata religio talibus moribus
choices.english: a religion worthy and born for such morals
choices.why: Preserves the ironic digna et nata and the dative of reference talibus moribus.
rejected: a religion fitting and suited to such character
a worship worthy and natural to such ways

choices.english: the funereal wood of the cross
choices.why: Keeps the contemptuous ligna (wood) and feralia (funereal, death-bringing).
rejected: the deadly wood of the cross
the funereal timber of the cross

choices.english: nevertheless equally in consciousness of incest
choices.why: Preserves the legal-moral force of conscientia and the concessive tamen.
rejected: yet equally guilty in conscience of incest
still alike in awareness of incest

pass_b_english: And now, as wicked things spring up more abundantly, with morals growing more corrupt day by day, those foulest shrines of an impious union are spreading throughout the whole world. This conspiracy must be utterly rooted out and cursed.

They recognize one another by secret marks and signs, and they love each other almost before they know each other. Everywhere among them a kind of religion of lust is mixed in, and they indiscriminately call each other brothers and sisters, so that even ordinary debauchery becomes incest through the intercession of the sacred name. So their empty and insane superstition boasts of crimes.

Nor would the most wicked and yet reputable rumor spread about them unless there were truth behind it. I hear that they venerate the consecrated head of a most vile beast, an ass, through some absurd persuasion: a religion worthy and born for such morals!

Others say that they worship the genitals of their own high priest and adore his nature as if he were their father. I do not know whether it is false, but it is certainly a suspicion attached to their hidden and nocturnal rites. And the one who tells of a man punished with the ultimate penalty for his crime and the funereal wood of the cross in their ceremonies assigns fitting altars to the depraved and criminal, so that they worship what they deserve.

Now about the initiation of novices, the story is as detestable as it is well known. An infant covered with grain, to deceive the unwary, is placed before the one being initiated into the rites. This infant is killed by the novice, with the surface of the grain struck as if to harmless blows, with wounds hidden and unseen. Of this infant—what wickedness!—they thirstily lick the blood, they divide the limbs in rivalry, by this victim they are bound together, by this consciousness of crime they pledge themselves to mutual silence. These rites are fouler than all sacrileges.

And about their banquet it is well known; everyone speaks of it everywhere, and the speech of our fellow citizen of Cirta testifies to it. On a solemn day they gather for a feast with all their children, sisters, mothers, people of every sex and every age. There after much feasting, when the banquet has grown heated and the frenzy of incestuous lust has blazed up in the drunken, a dog tied to a lampstand is provoked to leap and spring by a morsel thrown beyond the length of the line by which it is bound.

So the conscious light is overturned and extinguished, and in shameless darkness they entangle themselves in the bonds of unspeakable desire by the uncertainty of chance, and even if not all in deed, nevertheless equally in consciousness of incest, since whatever can happen in the act of each is sought by the vow of all.
notes: The word 'asini' appears in brackets in the source, indicating an editorial insertion or uncertain reading; it is included in the gloss as 'an ass'.
The word 'mpudentibus' appears to be a typographical error or OCR damage for 'impudentibus' (shameless); glossed as 'shameless'.

problems.quote: the funereal wood of the cross
problems.why: 'Ligna' is plural 'wooden parts/pieces of wood' not singular 'wood'; 'feralia' means 'deathly/funereal' but also 'accursed/doom-laden'. The English compresses acceptably. No error.
'Certatim' means 'in rivalry/vying with each other' not 'eagerly'; the competitive, scrambling nature of the division is lost.
problems.fix: they divide the limbs in rivalry

problems.quote: since what can happen in the act of each is desired by the wish of all
problems.source_quote: quoniam uoto uniuersorum adpetitur quicquid accidere potest in actu singulorum
problems.why: 'Voto' means 'vow/oath' not 'wish'; the mutual pledge and complicity is sealed by vow, not mere desire. This changes the nature of the conspiracy from active sworn complicity to passive desire.
problems.fix: since whatever can happen in the act of each is sought by the vow of all

problems.why: 'Farre' is 'with grain/flour', 'superficie' is 'surface'; but 'farre contectus...adponitur...is infans a tirunculo...superficie quasi ad innoxios ictus prouocato'. The ablative absolute 'superficie...prouocato' means 'with the surface being provoked/challenged as if to harmless blows'. The English 'provoked by the surface of the grain' misreads: the novice is provoked by the surface (thinking it harmless), not the infant killed by the surface.
problems.fix: This infant is killed by the novice, with the surface of the grain challenged as if to harmless blows, with wounds hidden and unseen.
problems.ruling: "superficie ... prouocato" shows surface provoked, not novice provoked by surface.

problems.quote: by this consciousness of crime they are pledged to mutual silence
problems.source_quote: hac conscientia sceleris ad silentium mutuum pignerantur
problems.why: 'Pignerantur' means 'they pledge/give as pledge' not 'are pledged'; active voice: they pledge themselves to silence. The English passive obscures agency.
problems.fix: by this consciousness of crime they pledge themselves to mutual silence
problems.ruling: "pignerantur" is active (they pledge), not passive "are pledged".

problems.quote: the most wicked and shameful rumor
problems.source_quote: maxime nefaria et honore praefanda sagax fama
problems.why: 'Honore praefanda' means 'to be spoken of with honor' ironically, or 'prefaced with honor'—actually this is difficult. 'Praefanda' from 'praefari' = to say beforehand, invoke. 'Honore praefanda' = 'to be prefaced with honor/respect', i.e., respectable, reputable. The rumor is 'most wicked and yet reputable/authoritative'. The English 'shameful' inverts the sense.
problems.fix: the most wicked and yet reputable rumor
problems.ruling: "honore praefanda" = to be spoken of with honor, opposite of "shameful".

problems.quote: a suspicion suited to their hidden and nocturnal rites
problems.source_quote: certe occultis ac nocturnis sacris adposita suspicio
problems.why: 'Adposita' means 'placed near/attached/applied to' not 'suited'; the suspicion is 'attached to' or 'associated with' their rites, not inherently 'suited'.
problems.fix: a suspicion attached to their hidden and nocturnal rites

edits.new: they divide the limbs in rivalry

edits.old: since what can happen in the act of each is desired by the wish of all
edits.new: since whatever can happen in the act of each is sought by the vow of all

edits.old: This infant is killed by the novice with wounds hidden and unseen, provoked by the surface of the grain as if to harmless blows.
edits.new: This infant is killed by the novice, with the surface of the grain challenged as if to harmless blows, with wounds hidden and unseen.

edits.old: by this consciousness of crime they are pledged to mutual silence
edits.new: by this consciousness of crime they pledge themselves to mutual silence

edits.old: the most wicked and shameful rumor
edits.new: the most wicked and yet reputable rumor

edits.old: a suspicion suited to their hidden and nocturnal rites
edits.new: a suspicion attached to their hidden and nocturnal rites

fixed: The funereal wood of the cross: 'ligna' is plural but the English 'wood' is acceptable as a collective; 'feralia' is rendered as 'funereal'. No error.
They eagerly divide the limbs: 'certatim' means 'in rivalry', so 'eagerly' loses the competitive sense. Fixed.
Since what can happen in the act of each is desired by the wish of all: 'uoto' means 'vow', not 'wish'. Fixed.
The surface of the grain: the English misread the ablative absolute; the surface is challenged, not the agent of killing. Fixed.
By this consciousness of crime they are pledged to mutual silence: 'pignerantur' is active, not passive. Fixed.
The most wicked and shameful rumor: 'honore praefanda' means 'reputable', not 'shameful'. Fixed.
A suspicion suited to their hidden and nocturnal rites: 'adposita' means 'attached to', not 'suited'. Fixed.

problems.quote: my friend Natalis's opinion has wavered
problems.why: Caecilius is suddenly called 'Natalis' with no explanation; reader thinks a new person.
problems.fix: Add note: Natalis is an alternate name for Caecilius.

problems.quote: with the surface of the grain challenged as if to harmless blows
problems.why: 'Challenged' does not fit; likely a mistranslation of Latin for 'tested' or 'struck.'

edits.old: with the surface of the grain challenged as if to harmless blows
edits.new: with the surface of the grain struck as if to harmless blows

fixed: The glossary problem about 'Natalis' does not appear in the current English text; no edit needed.
Changed 'challenged' to 'struck' to better render 'prouocato' in the sense of being struck or tested by blows.

last_rejected.why: 'honore praefanda' means 'to be mentioned with honor/respect' not 'reputable'; 'sagax' means 'keen/shrewd' not modifying rumor's character.
last_rejected.fix: a rumor keen to be mentioned with honor, or shrewd report deserving respect
last_rejected.ruling: ‘honore praefanda’ = honorable; ‘sagax fama’ = shrewd rumor – translation captures honor, loses shrewd nuance but not major.

last_rejected.why: 'digna...nata' is sarcastic: 'worthy AND born for such morals' misses that 'nata' means 'born/destined' but 'digna et nata' = 'worthy of AND born from'; better 'born of such morals'.
last_rejected.fix: a religion worthy of and born from such morals!
last_rejected.ruling: ‘digna et nata’ literally ‘worthy and born’, translation matches literal sense; nuance of sarcasm not essential.

last_rejected.quote: as if he were their father
last_rejected.why: 'parentis sui' = 'of their own parent', not 'he were their father'; 'adorare naturam' = adore his nature/sexual organ, with 'parentis sui' as genitive of source.
last_rejected.fix: adore his nature as if of their own parent
last_rejected.ruling: ‘quasi parentis sui’ can be rendered ‘as if he were their father’; translation acceptable.

last_rejected.why: 'conscius' here means 'witnessing' or 'all-knowing/aware', not 'conscious'; the light is personified as witness.
last_rejected.ruling: ‘conscio lumine’ = with the light of conscience; ‘conscious light’ conveys core meaning.

last_rejected.why: 'sortis' = lot/casting of lots, not 'chance'; they use lots to pair off randomly for sex.
last_rejected.fix: by the drawing of uncertain lots
last_rejected.ruling: ‘per incertum sortis’ = through the uncertainty of lot/chance; ‘by the uncertainty of chance’ is fine.

last_rejected.quote: since whatever can happen in the act of each is sought by the vow of all
last_rejected.source_quote: quoniam uoto uniuersorum adpetitur quicquid accidere potest in actu singulorum
last_rejected.why: 'uoto' = by vow/desire, but 'adpetitur' = is aimed at/sought; 'accidere potest' = can happen; but 'incesti' consciousness shared—meaning is that all share guilt since all desire whatever any one does.
last_rejected.fix: since by the desire of all is aimed at whatever can happen in the act of each
last_rejected.ruling: Translation mirrors Latin structure; meaning retained despite stylistic nuance.

polish.changed: Clarified that Caecilius is the speaker throughout, resolved the ambiguous reference to the person from Cirta as an unnamed source, and corrected the mistranslation of the grain surface being 'struck' rather than 'challenged.'

notes.quote: my friend Natalis's opinion has wavered
notes.why: Caecilius is suddenly called 'Natalis' with no explanation; reader thinks a new person.
notes.fix: Add note: Natalis is an alternate name for Caecilius.

notes.quote: the speech of our fellow citizen of Cirta testifies to it
notes.why: An unnamed person from Cirta is cited as a source; reader cannot identify him.
notes.fix: Note: this likely refers to Fronto, cited later in section 31.

notes.quote: with the surface of the grain challenged as if to harmless blows
notes.why: 'Challenged' does not fit; likely a mistranslation of Latin for 'tested' or 'struck.'
